key_concept: The male accessory duct system runs from the testis outward, while the infundibulum is the funnel-shaped part of the female oviduct (fallopian tube).
steps: Recall the male sperm transport pathway: seminiferous tubules → rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra.
Rete testis: a network of channels in the testis that receives sperm from the seminiferous tubules. It is male, so option (1) is a male structure.
Vasa efferentia: fine ductules that carry sperm from the rete testis to the epididymis. Male, so option (3) is a male structure.
Epididymis: a coiled tube on the posterior surface of the testis where sperm are stored and mature. Male, so option (2) is a male structure.
Infundibulum: the funnel-shaped part of the fallopian tube closest to the ovary. Its finger-like fimbriae collect the ovum after ovulation. It belongs to the female reproductive system.
Hence the infundibulum is not part of the male reproductive system, which matches the official answer.
why_not_others: Rete testis, vasa efferentia and epididymis are consecutive parts of the male intra-testicular and extra-testicular duct system, so all three are male structures.
common_trap: Students sometimes take 'infundibulum' to mean the pituitary stalk (also called infundibulum) and lose track of its reproductive meaning, or confuse vasa efferentia with a female structure because of its unfamiliar name.
time_saving_tip: Remember the male duct sequence 'Rete → Efferentia → Epididymis → Deferens'. Any option outside this chain (infundibulum, ampulla, isthmus, fimbriae) is part of the female oviduct.
